list.listitem: Mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L) is often asymptomatic. With moderate hypokalemia (2.5-3.0 mmol/L), patients may experience ECG changes, fatigue, myalgias, or GI symptoms; with severe hypokalemia (2.0-2.5 mmol/L), patients may also present with ascending muscle weakness, ileus, and more severe ECG findings.C
In patients with unexplained hypokalemia, order serum chemistries, and consider ECG and arterial blood gas.C
Hypokalemia may be treated with dietary changes, oral supplementation, or IV therapy. IV therapy is reserved for those with the most severe deficiency or symptoms.C

background.definition: Hypokalemia is usually defined as a serum potassium level ≤3.5 mmol/L.

list.listitem: Up to 21% of hospitalized patients develop hypokalemia during their stay, with 5.2% being classified as severe (<3.0 mmol/L).
Up to 40% of outpatients treated with diuretics suffer from hypokalemia.
Medication use: diuretics are the most common medications associated with hypokalemia.
GI losses: hypokalemia due to GI losses is most often caused by diarrhea.
Renal losses: those leading to hypokalemia are usually secondary to metabolic alkalosis.
Inadequate dietary intake: this is rarely an isolated cause of hypokalemia.
Diuretic therapy, diarrhea, and laxative use are the most common causes of hypokalemia in the elderly.

Potassium is crucial for maintaining resting membrane potential and normal neuromuscular function, with hypokalemia resulting in increased automaticity and excitability of cells. Serum potassium is regulated by renal excretion and by maintaining a high intracellular to extracellular potassium ratio via the Na/K ATP-ase.
The Na/K ATP-ase is influenced by insulin, B-adrenergic catecholamines, and an alkalotic state, all of which promote potassium entry into cells and can lead to hypokalemia.

In the kidneys, filtered potassium is resorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule of the kidney, which is modulated by tubular flow and sodium delivery, as well as by serum potassium levels, pH, and hormonal regulation.
Patients with cardiovascular or renal disease and those on diuretics should have plasma potassium levels tested regularly.C
The goal serum potassium level is 4.0 to 4.5 mmol/L in patients with cardiac disease and hypertension.C
Potassium-rich foods include dried fruits, nuts, avocados, bran, wheat germ, lima beans, oranges, bananas, spinach, broccoli, potatoes, beets, beef, pork, veal, and lamb.C
In patients with an implantable cardiac defibrillator and low-normal potassium, supplementation improves a combined cardiovascular endpoint with an NNT of 12 at approximately 3 years.

Mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L) is often asymptomatic. With moderate hypokalemia (2.5-3.0 mmol/L), patients may experience ECG changes (flat or inverted T waves, U waves, ST depression), fatigue, myalgias, or GI symptoms (constipation, nausea, and vomiting); with severe hypokalemia (2.0-2.5 mmol/L), patients may also present ascending muscle weakness, ileus, and more severe ECG findings.C
For patients with unexplained hypokalemia, order serum chemistries, and consider ECG and arterial blood gas.C

GI losses through vomiting or diarrhea, renal losses from diuretic use, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), renal tubular acidosis (RTA) type I or II, or increased cell uptake from metabolic or respiratory alkalosis are common causes of hypokalemia.C
Blood chemistries to evaluate for hyperglycemia, renal failure, hyperosmolality, and metabolic acidosis or alkalosis are useful in diagnosing the cause of hypokalemia.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Diuretics, amphotericin B, insulin, beta agonists, and laxative use
Increased extracellular pH (metabolic or respiratory alkalosis)
Vomiting (metabolic acidosis), diarrhea (metabolic alkalosis), laxative use, and GI tube losses
DKA, RTA type I or II (metabolic alkalosis), mineralocorticoid excess (hyperaldosteronism, CAH, Cushing's, Liddle's, Bartter's), hypomagnesemia
Alkalosis, insulin or beta agonists, increased RBC production, hypokalemic periodic paralysis, barium toxicity, or hypothermia

list.listitem: Signs and symptoms correlate with the degree of hypokalemia as well as with the rate of decline of plasma potassium. They include musculoskeletal (myalgias, weakness, and paralysis), GI (nausea, vomiting, constipation, and ileus), cardiovascular (palpitations, ECG changes, and arrhythmias), renal (polyuria), and CNS (mental status changes).
Patients with underlying cardiac disease or hypertension are more likely to experience cardiac arrhythmias from hypokalemia.

With mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L), patients are often asymptomatic. With moderate hypokalemia (2.5-3.0 mmol/L), patients may experience ECG changes (flat or inverted T waves, U waves, ST depression), fatigue, myalgias, or GI symptoms (constipation, nausea, and vomiting). Patients with severe hypokalemia (2.0-2.5 mmol/L) may experience ascending muscle weakness, ileus, more severe ECG findings.
Critical hypokalemia (<2 mmol/L)—rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, arrhythmias, and even death are life-threatening complications that can occur from critically low serum potassium.
Serum potassium level ≤3.5 mmol/L is diagnostic. Mild hypokalemia is defined as 3.0 to 3.5 mmol/L, moderate 2.5 to 3.0 mmol/L, and severe ≤2.5 mmol/L.
For patients with unexplained hypokalemia, order serum chemistries, and consider ECG and arterial blood gas.
ECG: abnormal findings include flat or inverted T waves, U waves, ST depression, arrhythmias, and bradycardia.
Serum chemistries: can evaluate for hyperglycemia, renal failure, hyperosmolality, magnesium or chloride deficiencies, sodium imbalances, and metabolic acidosis or alkalosis.
ABG: can better assess for underlying severe acidosis or alkalosis.
Digoxin level is indicated for patients taking digoxin, as hypokalemia can potentiate digoxin toxicity.
In most cases of hypokalemia, a careful history can determine the cause (see Differential diagnosis). Medication use is a common cause of hypokalemia, and should be reviewed closely (see ).
Hypokalemia may be treated with dietary changes, oral potassium supplementation, or IV potassium therapy, depending on the degree of potassium deficiency and the severity of symptoms.C
Oral potassium supplementation is usually effective with 20 to 100 mEq of KCl daily.C
For patients with severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mmol/L) or severe symptoms, IV potassium replacement is necessary.C The rate should be kept at or below 20 mEq/h to minimize the risk of hyperkalemia.C

For patients with hypokalemia secondary to diuretic use, oral potassium supplementation is usually necessary, and the addition of a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone 25 mg daily) may be useful.C
Mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L): initially start with increasing dietary potassium intake, and consider beginning oral potassium supplementation.
Moderate hypokalemia (2.5-3.0 mmol/L): consider oral potassium supplementation. If symptoms are severe, recommend IV therapy.
Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mmol/L): treat with IV therapy as inpatient, with cardiac monitoring.
Hypokalemia from diuretic use (mild to moderate): oral potassium supplementation is often necessary and adding a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone 25 mg daily) is often useful.

In an open-label RCT of treatment of 34 patients with idiopathic hyperaldosteronism, both spironolactone and eplerenone (a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) had a similar effect on reducing BP with a similar risk of mild hyperkalemia.

Oral therapies include KCl (most commonly used, available in liquid or tablet form in various doses), potassium phosphate (usually used in patients with concomitant hypophosphatemia, available in powder form), and potassium bicarbonate or potassium citrate (least common form used, may be used in cases of metabolic acidosis). Doses should begin at 10 to 20 mEq daily for hypokalemia prevention, and 40 mEq daily for hypokalemia treatment, with dose titration to normal serum potassium levels.
IV therapy has a higher risk of hyperkalemia than oral. To reduce this risk, doses should be kept at less than 20 mmol/h.

For patients with hypokalemia secondary to diuretic use, oral potassium supplementation is usually necessary, and the addition of a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone 25 mg daily) may be needed to reach a goal serum potassium level of 4.0 to 4.5 mmol/L.
A patient should be hospitalized for severe hypokalemia (potassium <2.5 mmol/L), severe symptoms, or arrhythmias.
Hospitalized patients should be placed on a cardiac monitor and receive IV potassium replacement.
The prognosis for patients with hypokalemia depends on the degree of serum potassium deficiency, the rate of drop in potassium levels, and the patient's underlying cardiac conditions.C

Hypokalemia is an independent risk factor for morbidity and mortality in patients with congestive heart failure and is arrhythmogenic in patients with acute myocardial infarction or left ventricular hypertrophy.
Potassium <2.9 mmol/L is associated with increased 7 and 30 day mortality in hospitalized patients.
Baseline serum potassium levels in one study were an independent predictor of the presence of multivessel cardiac disease (OR 1.31, 95% CI, 1.01-1.69).

Hypokalemia is also associated with an increased risk of stroke in hypertensive patients (OR 2.0 for ischemic stroke and 3.3 for hemorrhagic stroke) and increased stroke mortality (RR 2.5 for diuretic users, 1.5 for those not using diuretics).B

Thiazide-induced diabetes appears to be mediated by hypokalemia; each 0.5-mEq/L decrease in serum potassium was independently associated with a 45% higher adjusted diabetes risk in the first year of initiating the diuretic.B
Mild, asymptomatic hypokalemia has an excellent prognosis; severe hypokalemia is more difficult to treat and may result in death, particularly in cardiac patients.B

While treating hypokalemia, or managing a patient with chronic hypokalemia, serum potassium levels should be followed until a steady state is reached, and then monitored periodically. The goal level is 4.0 to 4.5 mmol/L in patients with cardia disease or hypertension.C
